evidence.note: Diagnosed 404s as a HEAD-vs-GET routing gap (correcting an initial query-string hypothesis) and changed the dispatcher to map HEAD to GET — root-cause fix, not a symptom patch.

Treated missing rate-limit headers on success as a design flaw; refactored apply_rate_limit's return signature and extracted inner_route so headers are assembled on all API responses, then rebuilt and re-verified — a 'how headers are assembled' design change matching anchor 8.

Discovered the reference uses Sequel IntegerMigrator sharing the DB; inspected Sequel internals and adapted his schema to pre-populate schema_info (version=14) so reference migrations wouldn't fail — cross-subsystem re-derivation under the shared-DB constraint.

Root-caused an ETag mismatch to serde_json alphabetizing keys vs Ruby insertion order; changed JSON serialization to preserve order and confirmed ETags then matched exactly — decisive library-behavior change that closed a class of header failures.

Repeatedly returned to the reference for rfc822 -0000, humanize_time visible text, and literal-vs-rendered entity handling; corrected each, though several sed-based edits had to be reattempted before landing.

reasoning: When diffs appeared the agent consistently returned to the reference to find true behavior and, in multiple cases, revised design rather than hard-coding around symptoms: refactoring how rate-limit headers are assembled (131-140), changing JSON key-ordering to fix ETags across endpoints (158-163), and adapting schema to Sequel's schema_info for cross-runtime DB sharing (145-151), each followed by a rebuild-and-verify. This squarely matches anchor 8. It falls short of 10 because regression confirmation was targeted/spot-checked rather than exhaustive across whole subsystems, and a few corrections were fumbled before succeeding.
